name: Design a Zero-Downtime Database Migration
intent: Move a live 5 TB production database to a new datacentre or cloud while the application keeps reading and writing, with proof that nothing was lost and a way back if it goes wrong.
codeTitle: a live migration with a snapshot, a change log, checksums and a rollback
finalIntro: A write reaching the old database, following the change stream to the new one, and the moment traffic moves.
prompt: Design the migration of a 5 TB Postgres database serving a busy application from one datacentre to a managed database in another cloud. The application may not go down for more than a few seconds, no committed write may be lost, and if the new system misbehaves after the switch, the team must be able to go back.
functional: Copy all the data to the new database from a consistent point in time
Keep the new database in sync with the writes that arrive during and after the copy
Prove the two databases hold the same data before switching
Move reads, then writes, to the new database in stages
Roll back to the old database without losing writes made on the new one
Retire the old system when the migration is done
nonFunctional: Writes are paused for seconds at most, not hours
No committed write is lost or applied twice
The copy must not slow down production traffic noticeably
Replication lag is below a few seconds before the cutover starts
Every row is accounted for, with checks that run while the system is live
The decision to go back stays possible for days after the switch
Ids created on the new database never collide with ids the old one handed out

firstAttempt.text: Schedule a maintenance window. Stop the application, dump the database, load the dump into the new one, change the connection string, and start the application again.
limits: At 200 MB/s a 5 TB copy takes about 7 hours, and the whole service is down for all of them
If the copy is started while the application keeps writing, rows copied early are already out of date when it ends
There is no check that the new database matches the old one, so a mistake is found by customers
After the switch the old database stops receiving writes, so going back means losing everything written since
The new database may hand out ids the old one already used, and one unlucky write overwrites a live row

steps.title: Copy a consistent snapshot while the old database keeps serving
steps.problem: Copying a 5 TB database takes hours, and copying rows from a live database gives a mixture of old and new states that never existed at one moment.
steps.fix: Take a consistent snapshot at one point in time, such as a base backup plus the log position it corresponds to, or an exported transaction snapshot, and copy that. Run the copy from a replica, in parallel by table and by key range, with a speed limit so production is not starved. Record the exact log position of the snapshot, because everything after it must be replayed. Copying live rows without a snapshot and a log leaves the copy wrong the moment a row changes after it was copied.
steps.tradeoff: The old database stays up and the copy is a true picture of one moment. It takes hours, uses network and disk, and from the first second the copy is already behind, so a second mechanism has to deal with the writes that arrive meanwhile.

steps.title: Stream the changes and let the new database catch up
steps.problem: During the hours of the copy the application made millions of writes, and the new database knows nothing about them.
steps.fix: Read the old database's change log, such as the Postgres write-ahead log through logical replication, starting at the snapshot position, and apply every entry to the new database in order. Applying must be safe to repeat, so that an entry replayed after a restart changes nothing. Keep going after the new database catches up, so that it follows the old one with a lag of seconds. Watch that lag as the main health number of the migration.
steps.tradeoff: The new database ends up current without stopping writes, and it stays current. The change log must be kept until it is consumed, which fills the old disk if the target falls behind. Apply speed must exceed the write rate, or the lag never closes.

steps.title: Verify continuously: counts, chunk checksums and shadow reads
steps.problem: Replication can silently drop or alter data through a bug, a type difference or a missed table, and nobody notices until the old system is gone.
steps.fix: Run checks all the time, not once. Compare row counts per table. Split each table into key ranges, compute a checksum per range on both sides and compare them, then dig into only the ranges that differ. Count the lag as it moves. Sample live reads: the application also asks the new database, compares the answer and logs a mismatch, but serves the old answer. A differing range is repaired by recopying it, and the cause is fixed before moving on.
steps.tradeoff: The mismatch is found while the old system is still the truth, when it costs nothing. Checksum passes read all the data on both sides, so they are throttled and run on replicas, and rows that change during a check can show up as false alarms that must be rechecked.

steps.title: Cut over in stages: reads first, then a short write freeze
steps.problem: Switching everything at once means any problem hits all traffic, and writes in flight during the switch can be lost or applied to the wrong database.
steps.fix: Put a connection router between the application and the databases. First move a small share of reads to the new database and grow it while watching errors and latency, with writes still going to the old one. When the lag is below the agreed threshold, such as two seconds, freeze writes on the old database, let the stream drain the last entries, confirm the positions match, and point writes at the new database. Unfreeze. The freeze is the drain time plus the flip, a few seconds. A big-bang switch without a drain leaves the entries still in the stream behind.
steps.tradeoff: Problems show up on a small share of traffic, and writes are never accepted by two databases at once. The router is a new piece to build and trust, and the freeze is real, so the application must hold writes briefly and retry them rather than fail.

steps.title: Handle ids and sequences, and replicate in reverse
steps.problem: If the new database starts its id counters from the snapshot, it hands out ids that the old database already issued after the snapshot, and the first inserts collide. Separately, once writes move, the old database goes stale and a rollback would lose everything written since.
steps.fix: Before the flip, move every sequence to a value well above the old maximum, for example a gap of a million, or use ids that cannot collide, such as ones generated by the application. After the flip, run the change stream the other way: the new database's writes are replicated back into the old one, so the old system stays current. With that in place, going back is the same short freeze in reverse, and no write is lost.
steps.tradeoff: Rolling back stays cheap and safe for days, which is what lets the team accept the cutover. The ids have a gap, and the old database must keep running with its cost and its upkeep. Reverse replication needs the same care as the forward one, including the schema matching in both directions.

steps.title: Watch, keep the way back open, then decommission
steps.problem: Declaring victory the moment the switch works throws away the safety net, and problems like a slow monthly job show up days later.
steps.fix: Keep reverse replication and the old database running through a soak period that includes the slowest cycles, such as a month-end report. Compare error rate, latency and the continuous checks to the baseline. Then stop the reverse stream, take a final backup of the old system, revoke its credentials, remove the old connection strings and the router rules, delete the replication slots (markers that make the old database keep its log for a consumer) so they stop holding log space, and finally shut the old database down. Record what was learned.
steps.tradeoff: A long soak is the cheapest insurance, at the cost of paying for two databases for weeks. Leaving the old system around forever is the real risk: it keeps credentials and data nobody maintains, and a forgotten replication slot can fill a disk.

failures.scenario: The change stream falls behind and never catches up
failures.impact: The old database keeps its log for the stream, the disk fills, and the old production system can stop.
failures.answer: Alert on the lag and on log disk use. Speed up the target by batching and parallel apply, pause the checksum jobs, or lower the copy speed. A slot that has fallen too far is dropped before it stops the source, and the migration restarts from a fresh snapshot.

failures.scenario: A checksum shows some ranges differ
failures.impact: Cutting over would silently lose or change rows, for example from a type conversion or a column the stream skipped.
failures.answer: Compare the differing ranges row by row to find the pattern, repair them by recopying, and fix the cause before cutting over. Recheck rows that changed during the check so a moving row is not counted as a fault.

failures.scenario: Sequences restart at the snapshot value
failures.impact: New rows get ids that already exist, so inserts fail or, worse, overwrite live rows.
failures.answer: Before the flip, set every sequence above the old maximum with a safety gap, and test it by inserting on the new database in a rehearsal. Prefer ids generated by the application, which cannot collide.

failures.scenario: The new database misbehaves an hour after the cutover
failures.impact: Latency is poor under real load and the team needs to go back, but writes since the flip exist only on the new system.
failures.answer: Reverse replication has kept the old database current, so the rollback is a freeze, a drain of the reverse stream and a flip of the router. Without reverse replication the same decision loses every write since the cutover, which is why it is built before the flip, not after.

failures.scenario: A write reaches both databases during the switch
failures.impact: The two databases accept different values for the same row, a split brain that is very hard to repair.
failures.answer: Only one database is the source of truth at any moment. The old one is made read-only (or fenced) before the new one accepts writes, and the router flips only after the stream has drained to the same position. A fencing token (a number that rises with each new owner, so that writes carrying an old number are refused) or a leader lease makes a late write from an old connection fail.

alternatives.title: How the target stays in sync

options.name: Stop-the-world dump and load
options.con: Hours of downtime for a 5 TB database

options.name: Snapshot plus change log
options.pro: No application changes, ordered, and exact once it drains
options.con: Needs logical replication or a CDC (change data capture) tool, and matching schemas

options.name: Dual-write from the application
options.con: A failed or reordered write on one side diverges silently, and the old rows still need a backfill

alternatives.pick: Snapshot plus a change log, with dual-write only as a read-comparison tool for the checks.

alternatives.title: How you verify

options.name: Row counts
options.con: A changed value keeps the count the same

options.name: Chunk checksums
options.pro: Find any differing range, and tell where to look
options.con: Read all the data on both sides

options.name: Sampled shadow reads
options.pro: Tests real queries on real traffic
options.con: Only covers what the application happens to read

alternatives.pick: All three: counts for speed, checksums for completeness, shadow reads for the queries that matter.

alternatives.title: How you cut over

options.name: Big bang
options.con: Everything is at risk at once, and the stream's last entries are dropped

options.name: Reads first, then a short write freeze
options.pro: Risk grows slowly, and the freeze is seconds
options.con: Needs a router and clients that can wait

options.name: Source-of-truth flip behind a feature flag (a configuration switch that changes behaviour without a deploy)
options.pro: A flip and a flip back are the same switch
options.con: The application must support both targets

alternatives.pick: Reads first, then a short freeze, with the flag if the application can take it.

alternatives.title: The way back

options.name: Restore from backup
options.con: Loses everything since the cutover and takes hours

options.name: Keep the old database stale
options.con: Rollback loses the writes made on the new system

options.name: Reverse replication
options.pro: The old database stays current, so rollback is a short flip
options.con: Another stream to build, run and check

alternatives.pick: Reverse replication through the soak period.

roles.label: Application
roles.description: The service that keeps reading and writing during the move.

roles.label: Router
roles.description: The connection router that decides which database gets reads and writes.

roles.label: Change stream
roles.description: The ordered log of changes, forward and in reverse.

roles.label: Copy and checks
roles.description: The snapshot copier, the verifier, the id fix and the decommission work.

roles.label: Databases
roles.description: The old and the new database.

quiz.question: A 5 TB Postgres database must move to another cloud. A copy at 200 MB/s takes about 7 hours, and the application keeps writing during that time. How do you end with a current copy and only seconds of downtime?
options: Dump and load the tables in parallel, so that the copy takes under an hour, and accept that hour as downtime
Copy each table live in turn, then replay the application's request logs afterwards to fix any rows that changed
Start dual writes from the application now, then backfill the older rows later with a one-off copy job
Copy a consistent snapshot with its log position, then apply the change stream from there until the lag is seconds
quiz.explanation: The snapshot gives one true moment in time, and the log from that position carries every later change in order, so the new copy catches up without stopping writes. A faster dump is still an hour of downtime. Live copying mixes states, and dual writes diverge silently when one side fails or reorders a write.

quiz.question: The change stream applies 6,000 entries per second. The old database takes 4,000 writes per second, and the target is 3 minutes behind (about 720,000 entries). The goal is a write freeze of only a few seconds. What should happen?
options: Freeze writes now, because the drain has to happen at some point and the stream is already fast enough to do it
Move all reads to the new database now, which removes the need to wait for the write lag between the databases to close
Wait about 6 minutes while the backlog shrinks by 2,000 a second, then freeze at a lag near 2 seconds
Pause the application's writes for 30 seconds, then compare the row counts and switch anyway
quiz.explanation: With no new writes, draining 720,000 entries takes about 2 minutes, far beyond the target. Waiting about 6 minutes shrinks the backlog to around 8,000 entries, which drains in a second or two. Moving reads does not touch the write lag, and a fixed pause with a count check can switch while entries are still in the stream.

quiz.question: A cutover is done and writes now go to the new database. Management wants to be able to go back at any time during the next two weeks, without losing the orders taken since the cutover. What must be in place?
options: Nightly backups of the new database, which can be restored onto the old servers if the team has to go back
A reverse change stream from the new database into the old one, built before the flip and kept running after it
Application dual writes to both databases after the cutover, so that the old one never goes stale
A read-only copy of the old database taken at the cutover, which is promoted if the team goes back
quiz.explanation: Reverse replication keeps the old system current, so going back is the same drain and flip in the other direction. A backup or a frozen copy loses all writes since that point and takes hours. Dual writes can diverge when one write fails, and may leave two sources of truth.
